title: Depression in adults
subject: psychiatry
summary: Screen with 2 questions and the PHQ-9, assess severity, bipolar history and suicide risk, offer psychological therapy for less severe depression and CBT, an SSRI or both for more severe depression, review within 1 to 2 weeks, continue 6 to 12 months after remission, and taper slowly when stopping.

sections.title: Recognise and assess
items: Ask: during the last month, have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless, or by having little interest or pleasure in doing things? If yes, assess fully (PHQ-2 then PHQ-9).

Judge severity by symptoms, duration and functional impairment, not a symptom count alone. NICE NG222: PHQ-9 below 16 is less severe (subthreshold or mild); 16 or more is more severe (moderate or severe).
Ask about past mood elevation (bipolar disorder), psychotic symptoms, alcohol and drug use, physical illness, previous episodes and treatment response, relationships, debt, work and isolation.
Always ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and intent. Refer urgently to specialist mental health services if there is considerable immediate risk (see Self-harm and suicide risk (adult)).

Look for physical contributors: hypothyroidism, anaemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, chronic pain, sleep apnoea, stroke, Parkinson's disease, and drugs such as corticosteroids, isotretinoin and interferon.

sections.title: Less severe depression (NICE NG222)
items: Discuss preferences; if the person does not want treatment, arrange active monitoring with a further assessment within 2 to 4 weeks.

First-line options: guided self-help (6 to 8 sessions), group CBT or behavioural activation, individual CBT or behavioural activation, group exercise, mindfulness or meditation, interpersonal therapy, counselling or short-term psychodynamic therapy.
Start with the least intrusive option. Do not routinely offer an antidepressant first line for less severe depression unless it is the person's informed preference.

sections.title: More severe depression
items: Offer, by preference: individual CBT plus an antidepressant (NICE's most effective option), individual CBT, behavioural activation, an antidepressant alone, interpersonal therapy, problem-solving, counselling, psychodynamic therapy or group exercise.

SSRIs are the first choice for most people (sertraline, escitalopram, citalopram, fluoxetine). Consider mirtazapine or an SNRI based on past response, preferred side-effect profile (sedation, weight, sexual function), comorbidity and interactions.
At risk of suicide: take overdose toxicity into account; do not routinely start tricyclics (except lofepramine); limit the quantity supplied.
Psychotic depression: refer to specialist services; consider an antidepressant plus an antipsychotic (for example olanzapine or quetiapine).
Severe, life-threatening depression (not eating or drinking, high suicide risk) or failure of other treatments: consider ECT in specialist services.
Depression with anxiety: usually treat the depression first.

sections.title: Starting, reviewing and continuing
items: Explain early side effects (nausea, anxiety, agitation, insomnia), that benefit usually appears within 4 weeks, and that missed doses can cause withdrawal symptoms.

Review within 2 weeks of starting; review at 1 week if aged 18 to 25 or at increased suicide risk, then again within 4 weeks. Watch for agitation and suicidal ideation, especially early and after dose increases.
No response after 4 weeks at a therapeutic dose (or 4 to 6 weeks of therapy): check adherence, diagnosis, substance use and social factors before changing treatment. Use the PHQ-9 to track response.

Continue the antidepressant for at least 6 months after remission (CANMAT 2023: 6 to 12 months; 2 years or more with risk factors such as recurrent or severe episodes or residual symptoms). Review at least every 6 months.
Older adults: watch for hyponatraemia (especially with diuretics), falls and interactions. With NSAIDs, aspirin or anticoagulants, consider gastroprotection because SSRIs increase bleeding risk.

sections.title: No or limited response
items: Options: increase the dose within the licensed range if tolerated; switch to another SSRI or to a different class (SNRI, mirtazapine); add psychological therapy or group exercise.

Combination strategies, ideally with specialist advice: add mirtazapine or trazodone to an SSRI; augment with aripiprazole, quetiapine, olanzapine, risperidone, lithium, lamotrigine or liothyronine. Vortioxetine is an option after 2 failed antidepressants.

Lithium augmentation: level 12 hours after the dose, usually at or above 0.4 and not above 1.0 mmol/L (0.4 to 0.6 mmol/L at 65 or over); check weight, renal and thyroid function and calcium before starting and at least every 6 months.
Never combine an MAOI with an SSRI, SNRI or tricyclic; switches to or from MAOIs need specialist input and a washout.

sections.title: Stopping antidepressants
items: Taper in steps, for example halving the dose each time, with smaller reductions (for example 25%) at low doses, allowing 1 to 2 weeks between steps. Take particular care with paroxetine and venlafaxine.
Fluoxetine 20 mg daily can often be stopped using a period of alternate-day dosing, because of its long half-life.

Withdrawal symptoms (dizziness, electric-shock sensations, anxiety, irritability, poor sleep) usually start within days and settle in 1 to 2 weeks but can last longer. If severe, restart the previous dose and taper more slowly.

sections.title: Special situations
items: Bipolar disorder or antidepressant-induced mania: do not give an antidepressant alone; seek psychiatric advice.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: weigh the risks of untreated depression against drug risks and seek perinatal psychiatry advice.
India: Tele-MANAS (14416 or 1-800-891-4416) offers free 24-hour tele-mental health support and referral.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Missing bipolar disorder, psychotic features or alcohol and drug misuse.
Stopping after a few weeks, or stopping abruptly.
Prescribing large quantities of a tricyclic to someone at risk of suicide.
Serotonin toxicity from combining serotonergic drugs (tramadol, linezolid, methylene blue, St John's wort, MAOIs); see Serotonin syndrome (serotonin toxicity).
Citalopram above 20 mg daily in people over 65 (QT prolongation).

drugs.name: Sertraline
drugs.dose: 50 mg orally once daily; increase in 50 mg steps at intervals of at least 1 week if needed; max 200 mg daily

drugs.name: Escitalopram
drugs.dose: 10 mg orally once daily; max 20 mg daily (65 or over: start 5 mg, max 10 mg)
drugs.notes: Dose-related QT prolongation; reduce in hepatic impairment.

drugs.name: Citalopram
drugs.dose: 20 mg orally once daily; max 40 mg daily (over 65 or hepatic impairment: max 20 mg)

drugs.name: Fluoxetine
drugs.dose: 20 mg orally once daily; max 60 mg daily
drugs.notes: Long half-life; many CYP2D6 interactions; can be activating.

drugs.name: Mirtazapine
drugs.dose: 15 mg orally at night; increase to 30 to 45 mg at night if needed
drugs.notes: Sedation, weight gain; useful with insomnia or poor appetite; less sexual dysfunction.

drugs.name: Venlafaxine (modified-release)
drugs.dose: 75 mg orally once daily; increase if needed; max 375 mg daily
drugs.notes: Raises blood pressure at higher doses; withdrawal symptoms common; more toxic in overdose than SSRIs.

drugs.name: Lithium (augmentation)
drugs.dose: Dose by plasma level: 12-hour level at or above 0.4 and not above 1.0 mmol/L (0.4 to 0.6 mmol/L at 65 or over)
drugs.notes: Specialist initiation. Levels 1 week after starting and after each change, then every 3 months in the first year. Toxicity with dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics.
